scope: Selected cases across the 1776–2026 research window. Thirteen entries: 12 primary-source case studies and one 1776 institutional-history context case. No claim of a complete 250-year transaction census.

definitions.policy: Constitutional provisions, legislation, administrative appointments, government contracts and enforceable settlements are distinguished.
definitions.direct: An explicit documented relationship between a monetary interest/payment and specified official action. The source must establish whether the relationship is an admission, finding, allegation, legal bargain or failed attempt.
definitions.money: Actual receipts, promised fees, nominal securities, authorization ceilings and prospective obligations are different units.

cases.title: French assistance and the choice of commercial alliance
cases.jurisdiction: United States federal action or constitutional framework; see source
cases.payer: French Crown, routed through Beaumarchais and Roderigue Hortalez and Company

money.status: Initial covert support described by Library of Congress; institutional historical synthesis, not a newly reconciled payment ledger

cases.policy: Model Treaty of 1776 and Franco-American commercial/alliance treaties of 1778
cases.mechanism: American need for overseas military supplies shaped negotiations over commercial terms and alliance. Congress adopted the Model Treaty on September 17, 1776; agreements with France followed in 1778.
cases.outcome: Financing and diplomacy interacted. This is foreign state support of the Revolution, not domestic campaign finance or proof of a purchased vote.
cases.evidence: Institutional historical synthesis linking finance, procurement and diplomacy; exact accounting status disputed in historical records.
cases.counterevidence: The State Department history records disagreement over whether early aid was a gift or loan. France also pursued strategic interests against Britain. Do not add repeated descriptions of the same funds or assume a dollar conversion.

biographical_scope.actor_role: Vergennes: French foreign minister; Beaumarchais: commercial intermediary; American commissioners negotiated assistance.
biographical_scope.continuity_boundary: Specific state-credit and treaty relationship, not evidence of an unbroken secret control structure through 2026.

cases.title: Plantation and shipping interests in slave-importation bargaining
cases.jurisdiction: United States federal action or constitutional framework; see source

money.status: No paid or promised political transfer quantified

cases.policy: Constitution Article I section 9; Article V
cases.mechanism: Madison records General Charles Cotesworth Pinckney defending slave imports through plantation output, shipping, consumption and revenue, and warning of lost South Carolina assent. Rutledge also tied consent to protecting imports. [E01]
cases.outcome: Congress could not prohibit covered importations before 1808. The text allowed a duty up to $10 per person; that ceiling is neither a verified collection nor a bribe. [E02]
cases.evidence: Direct recorded economic-interest argument and enacted constitutional protection; no check-to-vote trace.
cases.counterevidence: Mason opposed the trade; Sherman prioritized forming the Union despite disapproval. Economic incentives and constitutional bargaining were interwoven. [E01]

biographical_scope.documented: The debate expressly connects enslaved labor, rice-region demand and carrying trade to political bargaining. [E01]
biographical_scope.actor_role: Pinckney and Rutledge: South Carolina convention delegates.
biographical_scope.continuity_boundary: Protection was time-limited. These records identify historical interests, not modern descendants' liability, childhood causes or a continuous corporate ownership chain.

cases.title: Creditor claims and federal assumption of state war debts
cases.jurisdiction: United States federal action or constitutional framework; see source
cases.payer: United States, through statutory debt funding

money.status: Nominal statutory subscription ceiling, not cash paid

cases.mechanism: Hamilton opposed reducing purchasers' claims to their acquisition cost, arguing that transferable claims, contracts and borrowing terms supported public credit. Congress authorized exchange of qualifying state war-debt certificates for federal obligations. [E03,E04]
cases.outcome: Federal funding terms protected eligible certificate holders and assumed defined state liabilities. The $21.5 million ceiling was payable through certificates, not a $21.5 million cash lobbying fund. [E04]
cases.evidence: Strong fiscal distribution and creditor-policy connection; paid lobbying or a purchased vote not established.
cases.counterevidence: Hamilton presents the alternative of favoring original holders who sold cheaply, and argues against it on contract and public-credit grounds. [E03]

biographical_scope.documented: Revolutionary war financing generated claims traded between original holders and purchasers; the report distinguishes foreign contractual debt from domestic restructuring. [E03]
biographical_scope.continuity_boundary: Public-credit institutions connect finance and policy; no specific merchant/plantation fortune or modern successor ownership is traced here.

cases.title: Yazoo land interests, legislative corruption and purchaser protection
cases.jurisdiction: United States federal action or constitutional framework; see source
cases.recipient: Georgia treasury; legislators allegedly promised land interests

money.status: Georgia Company statutory purchase terms: $50,000 before grant plus $200,000 due November 1, 1795

cases.policy: Georgia sale act of January 7, 1795; repeal of February 13, 1796; Fletcher v. Peck (1810)
cases.mechanism: The complaint alleged Gunn, M'Allister and Walker promised legislators land shares for favorable votes. Georgia's repeal preamble separately declared corruption and participating legislators' purchase interests. [E05,E06]
cases.outcome: Repeal attacked the grants. The Court protected an innocent subsequent purchaser's vested rights; it did not adjudicate each alleged bribe. [E06]
cases.evidence: Legislative corruption finding plus specific judicially recorded allegations; neither an audited bribe total nor a criminal verdict.
cases.counterevidence: Peck disputed the promises and asserted lack of notice. Judicial reasoning protected purchasers rather than endorsing corruption. [E06]

biographical_scope.documented: Land-company ownership incentives reached legislative allocation of territory. The repeal contrasted $500,000 accepted consideration with an $800,000 rejected offer. [E05]
biographical_scope.actor_role: Named purchasers, Georgia legislators, governor and later courts.
biographical_scope.continuity_boundary: Speculation-to-law mechanism established at this scope; specific plantation profits, later heirs and current beneficiaries not traced.

cases.title: Bank publicity spending and failed federal recharter
cases.jurisdiction: United States federal action or constitutional framework; see source
cases.payer: Second Bank of the United States
cases.recipient: Printers/publication vendors; complete named payees unavailable in selected account

money.status: Approximate expenditure reported by Jackson for 1831–1832, not an independently audited exact total

cases.policy: Recharter bill veto; executive deposit-removal policy statement
cases.mechanism: Bank-funded circulation of favorable articles, congressional reports and speeches aimed at public opinion and charter renewal; the March 1831 resolution described public information about the bank. [E07]
cases.outcome: Jackson vetoed the bill on July 10, 1832. Its proposed $3 million bonus/$200,000 annual payment was not enacted by that bill. [E08]
cases.evidence: Direct reported institutional advocacy spending; recipient-level accounting and vote causation incomplete.
cases.counterevidence: Spending did not secure the charter. Jackson's adverse account also identifies independent charter-expiry and administrative reasons for deposit removal. [E07,E08]

biographical_scope.documented: A chartered bank used institutional resources to defend privileges; the veto discusses benefits to domestic and foreign stockholders. [E08]
biographical_scope.continuity_boundary: Institutional publicity is a comparable mechanism, not proof that a modern bank inherits this entity's acts or that Jackson's accusation is neutral accounting.

cases.title: Providence Tool: contingent compensation for a federal musket contract
cases.jurisdiction: United States federal action or constitutional framework; see source

money.status: Norris's claimed compensation; company disputed the amount; payment not established.
Trial judgment for Norris, subsequently reversed; not a verified disbursement.

cases.policy: July 1861 War Department contract: 25,000 muskets at US$20 each.
cases.mechanism: The Court's record attributes procurement to Norris's efforts under a contingent agreement and describes influential introductions to Secretary of War Simon Cameron.
cases.outcome: In 1864 the Supreme Court held the compensation agreement unenforceable on public-policy grounds and remanded for a new trial.
cases.evidence: Primary documentary record; evidentiary qualifications stated with the outcome
cases.counterevidence: The rule rested on the agreement's tendency, without requiring proof of improper means. This is neither a proved bribe to Cameron nor proof that the musket contract itself was canceled.
cases.biographical_scope: Company: Rhode Island corporation supplying arms. Norris: intermediary. Cameron: Secretary of War.

cases.title: Crédit Mobilier: benefits to James Brooks within a subsidized railroad enterprise
cases.jurisdiction: United States federal action or constitutional framework; see source
cases.payer: Thomas C. Durant / Crédit Mobilier; later issuance arranged through Sidney Dillon
cases.recipient: Charles H. Neilson, named holder; House committee found James Brooks the beneficial owner

money.status: Brooks paid for 100 Crédit Mobilier shares transferred December 26, 1867.
Union Pacific bonds accompanying that transaction; stated securities amount, not cash.
Union Pacific stock accompanying that transaction; stated securities amount, not market value.
Price of 50 additional shares issued to Neilson February 29, 1868; financed by Dillon. Committee described their value as US$15,000–20,000; repayment unresolved.

cases.policy: Pacific Railroad Act, July 1, 1862, §§1, 5–6: Union Pacific charter and repayable federal bond aid.
cases.mechanism: The committee found the additional shares secured Brooks's official favor. Brooks and Alley denied the alleged promise to influence the Democratic side; the committee relied on surrounding circumstances too.
cases.outcome: February 27, 1873: House censured Ames and Brooks; Brooks vote 174–32. The adopted resolution condemned use of his offices to obtain stock.
cases.evidence: Primary documentary record; evidentiary qualifications stated with the outcome
cases.counterevidence: The committee did not find corrupt intent in the other previously discussed House purchasers. Later share transactions cannot establish that they caused the earlier 1862 statute; no specific subsequent roll-call purchased by Brooks's benefits is identified here.
cases.biographical_scope: Brooks: Representative and government director of Union Pacific; Dillon: Crédit Mobilier president.

cases.title: Fort Sill trading appointment: Evans–Marsh–Belknap payments
cases.jurisdiction: United States federal action or constitutional framework; see source
cases.payer: John S. Evans → Caleb P. Marsh → William W. Belknap
cases.recipient: Marsh, intermediary; Belknap, Secretary of War

money.status: October 8, 1870 Evans–Marsh contract, payable quarterly; later terms could change.
Receipt by Belknap on or about November 2, 1870, alleged in Article IV, specification 1.

cases.policy: Appointment of Evans as Fort Sill post trader on October 10, 1870, and continued tenure.
cases.mechanism: House articles expressly tied payments to appointment and retention; Article III alleged Marsh passed half to Belknap.
cases.outcome: August 1, 1876: Senate acquitted on every article because no guilty vote reached two-thirds.
cases.evidence: Primary documentary record; evidentiary qualifications stated with the outcome
cases.counterevidence: Charges are not a conviction. The official compilation records 22 not-guilty votes based on jurisdiction and three on evidence. Annual rates changed; no extrapolated multi-year total is asserted. This concerns administrative patronage, not proof of purchasing a statute.
cases.biographical_scope: Evans: trader; Marsh: intermediary; Belknap: Secretary of War.

cases.title: Doheny–Fall: US$100,000 and Elk Hills oil leases
cases.jurisdiction: United States federal action or constitutional framework; see source
cases.payer: Edward L. Doheny, through his son
cases.recipient: Albert B. Fall, Secretary of the Interior

money.status: Delivered November 30, 1921; demand note given; no principal or interest repayment reported in the opinion.

cases.policy: Pan American contracts of April 25 and December 11, 1922; Naval Petroleum Reserve No.1 leases of June 5 and December 11, 1922.
cases.mechanism: The Supreme Court sustained findings that Doheny corruptly secured Fall's influence and official action; Fall collusively dominated negotiations.
cases.outcome: February 28, 1927: cancellation upheld; contracts and leases held illegal and void.
cases.evidence: Primary documentary record; evidentiary qualifications stated with the outcome
cases.counterevidence: Companies argued loan, not bribe. Civil rescission did not require statutory criminal bribery or government financial loss. This opinion is not a criminal conviction of Doheny. Elk Hills is the California transaction, not Sinclair's Wyoming Teapot Dome lease.
cases.biographical_scope: Doheny controlled the two Pan American companies and served as Petroleum Company's president, then board chairman.

cases.title: Tobacco Master Settlement Agreement: lawful payments exchanged for specified claim releases and public-health restrictions
cases.jurisdiction: 46 U.S. states, District of Columbia and five U.S. territories; not a federal statute
cases.payer: Original participating manufacturers Philip Morris Inc., R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co., Lorillard Tobacco Co. and Brown & Williamson; subsequent participating manufacturers also assumed obligations.
cases.intermediary: Nationwide escrow account and independent auditor; the 2007 judicial opinion identifies PricewaterhouseCoopers as auditor at that time, not necessarily today.
cases.recipient: The settling governments, allocated under the agreement; no claim that attorneys general received the money personally.

money.period: 1998 agreement; scheduled/estimated aggregate through 2025 as described by CRS in November 1999
money.type: Civil settlement payment obligations, subject to the agreement's calculations and adjustments
money.status: Agreed prospective amount, not verified cumulative cash received
money.overlap: Do not add the separate earlier settlements with Florida, Minnesota, Mississippi and Texas to this amount. Do not describe this as a lobbying fee or criminal bribe.

cases.policy: Master Settlement Agreement, implemented through state litigation and consent-decree enforcement.
cases.mechanism: The Illinois appellate court describes dismissal and release of specified government claims in exchange for annual payments and marketing concessions. Pennsylvania's official summary documents youth-targeting and advertising restrictions, document access, and limits on opposing youth-access measures.
cases.outcome: An enforceable settlement changed participating manufacturers' conduct and settled government claims. This is direct money-for-defined-legal-consideration, not evidence that companies bought a federal law.
cases.evidence: PRIMARY_LEGAL_BARGAIN: judicial account of the agreement, official state enforcement summary, and contemporaneous Congressional Research Service analysis.
cases.counterevidence: The broader federal McCain tobacco bill failed on June 17, 1998. CRS distinguishes that proposal from the narrower MSA. Pennsylvania's summary expressly preserves criminal prosecution; the agreement was not general criminal immunity.
cases.limits: No inference that all tobacco regulation was purchased. The US$206 billion is a dated projection/obligation description, not a present receipt reconciliation. Individual and federal claims must not be silently folded into the settling governments' releases.
cases.biographical_scope: Manufacturers negotiated with state attorneys general as defendants and public litigants. The legal bargain and payment machinery, rather than personal ancestry, establish the relationship.

cases.title: Tigua–Scanlon–Abramoff: paid access and a failed casino amendment
cases.jurisdiction: U.S. Congress; proposed amendment to the Help America Vote Act
cases.payer: Ysleta del Sur Pueblo, commonly called the Tigua tribe
cases.intermediary: Michael Scanlon and his Capitol Campaign Strategies business; secret fee-sharing with lobbyist Jack Abramoff
cases.recipient: Scanlon/CCS and Abramoff; Ney's corrupt benefits are separately documented, not an allocation of the full tribal fee.

money.period: 2002 casino-reopening engagement, described in Senate Report 109-325
money.status: Reported paid by the Senate investigation
money.overlap: The US$1,850,000 secret share below is contained within these fees; do not add them.

money.period: Same engagement; Abramoff's January 3, 2006 plea admission
money.type: Scanlon's undisclosed kickback/fee share to Abramoff
money.status: Admitted receipt; not the report's higher projected partner share
money.overlap: Approximately half the project's actual net profit, not half the gross US$4.2 million; not an itemized Ney bribe total

cases.policy: Requested non-election amendment to election-reform legislation to permit the Tigua casino to reopen.
cases.mechanism: The Senate traces paid fees and concealed sharing to an unsuccessful reopening plan. Ney separately admitted attempts to insert four client-requested amendments into HAVA in exchange for benefits.
cases.outcome: The Tigua casino-reopening effort failed despite the payments. Ney's September 15, 2006 announcement concerned a signed agreement to plead guilty; it was not yet the court's entry of that plea.
cases.evidence: PRIMARY_DOCUMENTED_FAILED_INFLUENCE: Senate investigation using financial records and testimony, plus admitted corrupt official conduct in signed plea documents.
cases.counterevidence: The tribe did not know of Scanlon's secret payment to Abramoff. It must not be labeled a knowing participant in that concealed arrangement.
cases.limits: Ney's broader stream of benefits is not an exact allocation to this amendment. Do not add unrelated clients, total travel costs or other casino projects. Promised access did not guarantee passage.
cases.biographical_scope: Abramoff was a federal lobbyist and Scanlon his concealed business partner. Ney chaired the House Administration Committee from 2001 to January 2006, a relevant legislative access point.

cases.title: Cunningham: contractor payments exchanged for federal appropriations and contract intervention
cases.jurisdiction: United States Congress and federal defense procurement
cases.payer: Several defense-contractor coconspirators; DOJ separately identifies Mitchell Wade and Brent Wilkes. The aggregate is not assigned entirely to either man.
cases.intermediary: Direct cash, property transactions and in-kind benefits; no single intermediary accounts for all payments.

money.period: Bribes admitted in the November 28, 2005 plea; precise first payment date is not established by the two selected DOJ sources
money.type: Aggregate bribes, including cash and noncash benefits from several coconspirators
money.status: Admitted by recipient in guilty plea; sentencing reported March 3, 2006
money.overlap: Includes, rather than adds to, the separately described Wade payments. Tax restitution and forfeiture are not additional influence spending.

money.amount_text: More than US$1 million; the cited DOJ description does not supply a complete cash/noncash allocation
money.period: Pre-plea conduct described in the Attorney General's March 27, 2008 remarks; exact disbursement dates not stated there
money.type: Wade's illegal payments to Cunningham; the DOJ wording describes cash, antiques and a boat without a complete transaction allocation
money.status: DOJ reports Wade's conviction and his firm's resulting federal contracts
money.overlap: Subset/counterpart evidence for the larger Cunningham case, not a second independent sum

cases.policy: Federal appropriations and execution of defense contracts; the selected releases do not identify every appropriation line or award number.
cases.mechanism: Cunningham admitted that the benefits were exchanged for official action influencing appropriations and contract execution for contractor owners. The Attorney General identifies Wade's firm's receipt of federal contracts as resulting from illegal payments, and describes Wilkes' contract-steering relationship.
cases.outcome: Recipient pleaded guilty November 28, 2005 and received a 100-month sentence March 3, 2006. This supports a proven procurement/appropriations corruption mechanism, not a price for all U.S. defense policy.
cases.evidence: ADMITTED_CRIMINAL_EXCHANGE: DOJ's account of the plea and sentence, corroborated by the Attorney General's account of contractor convictions.
cases.counterevidence: The prosecutions and sentence show institutional detection and sanction. No selected evidence establishes that every associated contract lacked legitimate deliverables or that every campaign contribution by contractors was corrupt.
cases.limits: Do not publish an unsupported US$150 million award total or a precise beginning date from these sources. A quoted bribe-menu schedule is not an audited list of completed payments and is not used as the case total. Later clemency or appellate developments were not assessed in this bounded historical mechanism review.
cases.biographical_scope: Cunningham was a sitting congressman; the benefiting coconspirators were majority owners of defense contractors. Their official procurement relationship is material. No childhood or family-life inference is used.

cases.title: FirstEnergy and the Householder enterprise: nuclear bailout enacted, protected, then partly repealed
cases.jurisdiction: Ohio state legislation; federal criminal enforcement
cases.payer: FirstEnergy Corp. and related energy companies in the Householder scheme; the scheme aggregate is not allocated entirely to one payer legal entity by these releases.
cases.intermediary: Generation Now, a 501(c)(4), and the Householder enterprise; other 501(c)(4) entities helped conceal payments.
cases.recipient: Generation Now and the enterprise supporting Larry Householder's political power, allied candidates and personal benefits; not US$61 million paid solely into Householder's personal account.

money.type: Scheme-level bribes received through the enterprise
money.status: Proven at the 2023 Householder trial as reported by DOJ
money.overlap: Quarterly US$250,000 transfers and individual personal benefits are components, not additions. The US$230 million DPA penalty is a later sanction, not lobbying expenditure or the law's purchase price.

cases.policy: Ohio House Bill 6 nuclear bailout and effort to defeat the referendum seeking its repeal; later House Bill 128.
cases.mechanism: DOJ reports bribe-funded electoral support, Householder's official assistance in passing HB6, and efforts defeating the repeal initiative. FirstEnergy separately admitted payments for specific nuclear-legislation action in its July 22, 2021 deferred prosecution agreement.
cases.outcome: HB6 passed and the referendum was defeated. HB128 repealed the nuclear-credit payment and corresponding customer-charge provisions, effective June 30, 2021. Householder was convicted in March 2023 and sentenced June 29, 2023.
cases.evidence: ADMITTED_AND_TRIAL_PROVEN_EXCHANGE: corporate DPA admissions plus jury conviction, with legislative-service confirmation of the later statutory reversal.
cases.counterevidence: The nuclear subsidy did not remain permanently secure: HB128 removed it. HB128 was a partial change, so this record does not claim that all HB6 provisions disappeared. Enforcement and repeal limit any inference of complete or irreversible corporate control.
cases.limits: The nearly US$61 million is a conspiracy aggregate, not a per-vote price. Corporate admissions do not by themselves establish every executive's individual guilt. This bounded review reports the dated trial, agreement and legislation rather than asserting that every later appeal or proceeding has ended.
cases.biographical_scope: FirstEnergy was a public utility holding company; Householder used the enterprise to build support for his speakership. Campaign strategist Jeffrey Longstreth and lobbyist Juan Cespedes pleaded guilty, according to DOJ's 2023 account.
